clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant stromal dystrophy of abnormal corneal lipid deposition, linked to UBIAD1 mutations
Corneal crystals are present in only about half of cases, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis
Findings evolve with age: central crystalline haze, then a dense arcus lipoides, then diffuse stromal clouding
It is associated with systemic hyperlipidaemia, which should be screened for and managed
Vision declines slowly, and glare is a common complaint
Management includes lipid assessment and, for visually significant disease, superficial ablation or keratoplasty
reference.pathophysiology: Schnyder corneal dystrophy arises from mutations in the UBIAD1 gene, causing abnormal local metabolism and accumulation of cholesterol and phospholipids within the corneal stroma. This lipid deposition produces corneal crystals (when present), a prominent arcus and progressive stromal haze. Although the corneal defect is local, affected individuals frequently have systemic dyslipidaemia, so the cornea can be a marker of a broader lipid abnormality.
additionalDifferentials: Other crystalline keratopathies (for example cystinosis, monoclonal gammopathy, drug deposits)
Bietti crystalline dystrophy (retinal, with corneal crystals)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of crystals, arcus and stromal haze
Fasting lipid profile to assess systemic hyperlipidaemia
UBIAD1 genetic testing where confirmation is needed
Family history and examination of relatives
redFlags: Progressive visual loss or disabling glare
Features suggesting an alternative crystalline keratopathy
Rapid change atypical for a slowly progressive dystrophy
reference.prognosis: Vision declines slowly over decades; systemic lipid management is important, and superficial ablation or keratoplasty can help visually significant disease, though deposits may recur.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because crystals are absent
Confusing it with other crystalline keratopathies
Missing the autosomal dominant family history
management: Screen for and manage systemic hyperlipidaemia with lipid-lowering therapy such as statins plus lifestyle measures, since the cornea signals a broader lipid disorder
Manage glare and photophobia conservatively with tinted lenses while vision remains adequate
For visually significant stromal opacity offer superficial or phototherapeutic keratectomy, or lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty in advanced disease
Counsel that lipid deposits may recur in the cornea or graft after surgery, requiring ongoing review
Monitor visual acuity and corneal opacity over time with slit-lamp examination and corneal imaging
Coordinate care between ophthalmology and lipid or metabolic services
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant UBIAD1 dystrophy and examine relatives
